A1.topic: add rate limiting to public API endpoints

evidence.concreteness: Every requirement carries hard numbers: '<= 2ms p99 overhead under 1000 RPS', '~200 RPS deny rate, Redis CPU < 30%', three-state flag with named values 'off/shadow/enforce', explicit Lua-script size '<20 lines'.
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Frontmatter notes 'source_proposals: 2' and 'debate-transcript'; the text reconciles tensions (fail-open default vs. security-sensitive endpoints, monolithic v1 module vs. future growth) with named rationale rather than averaging.
evidence.coverage: Functional + non-functional + acceptance + open-questions + risks all present and tight; misses some adjacent concerns (client-facing headers like X-RateLimit-*, tiered billing limits, threat-model breadth) that the alternative output covers.
evidence.actionability: AC-5 reads 'one production endpoint runs in enforce mode for 7 consecutive days with zero p99 regression' — concrete done-ness; runbook contents (emergency disable, raise specific limit, swap backend) are itemized so an engineer can start tomorrow.
evidence.provenance: Frontmatter cites convergence_score and debate transcript; OQ-1 explicitly references 'confirmed via codebase scan'; R-4 cites 'greenfield risk - no existing rate-limit code in the repo' as constraint-derived rationale.

A1.overall_observation: Crisp, opinionated, decision-forward spec with explicit constraints traced to debate and codebase scan; scope is narrower than A2 but every claim is measurable and immediately implementable.

A2.topic: add rate limiting to public API endpoints

evidence.concreteness: Has many concrete details (X-RateLimit-* header set, '<2ms p99', '±5% accuracy', bucket-key format 'rl:{tier}:{key_id}:{window_id}') but some NFRs hedge ('appropriate to the requester's tier') and several requirements remain shape-only without thresholds.
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Five distinct personas (Architect, Analyzer, Frontend, Backend, Security) surface real tensions — fail-open vs. fail-closed, exposing X-RateLimit-* vs. hiding it from attackers, per-IP vs. distributed-botnet limits — and each persona pushes back on different framings.
evidence.coverage: Most comprehensive of the two — threat model, header contract, SDK retry guidance, compliance hooks (SOC2/PCI), webhook/long-poll edge cases, three driver framings (abuse/capacity/commercial) all explicitly enumerated.
evidence.actionability: AC list is solid (rates, headers, fail-open under killed-Redis) but 'Open Questions' remain unresolved at the end (driver, tier definitions, header policy) meaning a reader cannot start work without another conversation.
evidence.provenance: Codebase scan documented in Phase 0 (no FastAPI/Flask/etc., no existing rate-limit code); open questions explicitly tie back to the 'codebase mismatch' finding; every persona references prior context.

A2.overall_observation: Encyclopedic and well-structured but the breadth keeps several decisions open at the end; reads as a discovery document rather than a finalized spec, so actionability lags despite richer coverage.

B1.topic: post-mortem: staging deployment broke at 3am, manual revert was the only mitigation

evidence.concreteness: Specific thresholds where they matter: 'every event has >=2 independent sources', 'exposure window >30m escalate as separate finding', 'four control-gap prevention items: automated rollback, deploy gating, off-hours guardrail, paging on staging-only failure'.
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Frontmatter declares 'agents: [opus:analyzer, sonnet:security]' and the body explicitly splits 'two control loops failed — deploy-gate loop and mitigation loop' with parallel investigation tracks; an unresolved tension on blast-radius depth is flagged rather than papered over.
evidence.coverage: Solid on framework + investigation + prevention + communication; thinner than B2 on backend failure-mode taxonomy, on-call ergonomics, security audit-trail specifics, and architectural fitness functions — those workstreams are mostly compressed into single bullets.
evidence.actionability: Investigation steps are numbered and orderable; prevention items have named owners-and-due-dates as an acceptance criterion; weekly status epic provides cadence so a reader can immediately schedule the next step.
evidence.provenance: Frontmatter cites 'convergence_score: 0.72' and a debate transcript path; OQ-1 explicitly notes 'residual tension from debate; convergence not reached'; control-loop framing is presented as derived from the parallel-track analysis rather than asserted.

B1.overall_observation: Disciplined, leverage-focused post-mortem spec that names two control loops and forces class-vs-case rating; concise to a fault — coverage of backend/security/architect lenses present in B2 is compressed.

B2.topic: post-mortem: staging deployment broke at 3am, manual revert was the only mitigation

evidence.concreteness: Strong measurable NFRs ('MTTR <= 15 min off-hours', '>= 90% deploys with automated rollback engaging in 5 min', '30-day log retention'); but some FRs remain procedural ('use structured method', 'enumerate every change').
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Five fully fleshed personas (Analyzer, Security, DevOps, Backend, Architect) each take genuinely different stances — security on signed-revert vs devops on single-command-revert is reconciled with 'pre-sign known-good artifacts at deploy time'.
evidence.coverage: Most comprehensive of the two — failure-mode taxonomy, on-call ergonomics with burnout/HR support, audit-trail/credential review, architectural fitness functions, communications, compliance (SOC2), psychological safety — all enumerated.
evidence.actionability: AC-1 through AC-7 are testable, NFR targets are numeric, sprint cadence implied via 'hotfix/short-term/architectural' horizons; but 7 open questions remain unresolved, so 'immediately start work' is gated.
evidence.provenance: Each persona traces to a documented question in Phase 1, and the feasibility matrix shows cross-persona derivation; lacks an explicit debate transcript or convergence score — provenance is internal narrative rather than artifacted.

B2.overall_observation: Wide-coverage discovery doc with strongly differentiated persona voices and reconciled tensions; would benefit from compressing open questions into decisions before handing off to design.

evidence.concreteness: Hard numbers everywhere: '50-PR release in <=60s', '<=$1 inference cost', '>=70% finalized changelogs ship with <=30% line-diff', 'p95 cost <=$0.75', WCAG 2.1 AA with axe-core checks, '7-day retention'.
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Frontmatter shows 'proposal_count: 2' and convergence; the spec names competitor wedges (What The Diff, Release.com, GitHub native) and resolves tensions (BYO-key vs hosted, persona-tuning on/off via flag, GitHub App vs CLI/Action) with explicit deferral rationale.
evidence.coverage: Strong on personas + FRs + NFRs + AC + success metrics + MVP scope with explicit out-of-scope list; lighter on traceability/hallucination mitigation, redaction layer, and audit logging that C2 makes feature-blocking.
evidence.actionability: MVP scope with 7 explicit in-scope and 7 explicit out-of-scope items, each with reason ('Reason: GitHub App is the wedge'); AC integration-test assertions cite axe-core, network-mock, and vendor-pricing fixtures — engineer can scaffold the test plan today.
evidence.provenance: Competitor analysis (What The Diff, Release.com, GitHub) cited as the source of the wedge framing; deferral triggers explicit ('>=5 enterprise prospects', '>=3 dogfood users'); convergence_score documented in frontmatter.

C1.overall_observation: Tight, market-aware MVP spec with measurable thresholds and explicit no-list; under-indexes on traceability/redaction/audit trail relative to the trust-risk that C2 prioritizes as feature-blocking.

evidence.concreteness: Many measurable targets ('3-5 bullets', '100-PR cap', '<=15s median for 50 PRs', '<=$0.50/release', '>=60% releases', '<=1% unverifiable claims', '5-40% edit distance window'); some are still hedged ('observably different phrasing').
evidence.adversarial_diversity: Five distinct personas (Architect, Frontend, Backend, Analyzer, PM) with genuinely different framings — Architect pushes 'transformer, not system of record', Frontend pushes 'trust through traceability', Analyzer surveys 5 competitors and flags trust-collapse as the existential risk.
evidence.coverage: Most comprehensive — input adapters (3), redaction with allowlist/denylist, traceability/source citations, tone presets, audit log with 90-day retention, provider abstraction, accessibility, security-embargo carve-out, success metrics including edit-distance window.
evidence.actionability: Strong sprint-by-sprint plan (Sprint 0/1/2/3 with story points) and 12 FRs + 9 NFRs + 8 ACs that are testable; but 7 open questions are flagged for sprint-1 decision so immediate-start is gated by those.
evidence.provenance: Phase 0 reasoning explicit ('signal_A=false, signal_B=false, signal_C=false -> SKIP'); analyzer cites 5 competitor reference points; Phase 3 feasibility matrix derives the 'redaction + traceability ship together' decision from cross-persona pressure.

C2.overall_observation: Most thorough of the six; trust contract (traceability + redaction) elevated to feature-blocking with strong rationale; sprint plan and persona reasoning are top-tier, though open questions remain and length impacts immediate-start usability.

A.rationale: A1 edges A2 (22 vs 21) on actionability and concreteness — every requirement in A1 has a measurable threshold and the open questions are bounded so an engineer could start the integration test and runbook today, while A2's broader coverage leaves the dominant driver (abuse/capacity/commercial), tier definitions, and header policy explicitly open. A2 wins coverage by a clear margin (threat model, SDK guidance, compliance hooks) but pays for it with less decision-forward output.

B.rationale: B2 (21) edges B1 (19) primarily on coverage and adversarial diversity — five fully-fleshed personas surface tensions (signed-revert vs single-command-revert reconciled via pre-signing) and the spec spans failure-mode taxonomy, on-call ergonomics including psychological safety, audit-trail completeness, and architectural fitness functions. B1's strength is its two-control-loop discipline and class-vs-case prevention rating, but it compresses the backend/security/architect lenses into single bullets.

C.rationale: C1 and C2 both score 22 with very different shapes: C1 wins concreteness and actionability via market-positioned MVP scope with explicit in/out lists and named competitor wedges, while C2 wins adversarial diversity and coverage via five distinct personas and a trust-contract framing (traceability + redaction feature-blocking) that C1 under-indexes on. A team prioritizing speed-to-build would pick C1; a team prioritizing trust/hallucination risk would pick C2.
